title: Bits: Power of Two
oneLiner: A power of two has exactly one 1 bit, and n & (n - 1) clears the lowest 1 bit, so n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0 answers it in O(1).
keyTakeaway: n & (n - 1) removes n's lowest set bit. A power of two has only one set bit, so the result is 0 exactly for powers of two. The n > 0 check is not optional: 0 & -1 is 0, and in C# int.MinValue & int.MaxValue is 0 too, yet neither is a power of two.
explanation:
Return true if n is a power of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 2^30 for a 32-bit int. Negative numbers and 0 are not.

The loop answer divides by 2 while n is even and checks whether you end at 1, which is O(log n). The bit answer is O(1). In binary, a power of two is a single 1 followed by zeros: 8 is 1000, 64 is 1000000. Subtracting 1 turns that 1 into 0 and every 0 below it into 1: 8 - 1 = 7 is 0111. They share no 1 bits, so 8 & 7 = 0. For a number with two or more 1 bits, such as 12 (1100), subtracting 1 only changes the lowest one and the zeros below it (11 is 1011), so the higher 1 bits survive the AND: 12 & 11 = 8, not 0. That's the general rule: n & (n - 1) is n with its lowest set bit cleared.

Why n > 0 matters. 0 & (0 - 1) = 0 & -1 = 0, so without the check 0 counts as a power of two. In C#, int.MinValue is -2,147,483,648, whose two's complement pattern is a 1 in bit 31 followed by 31 zeros, a single set bit just like a power of two. n - 1 wraps round to int.MaxValue (0 followed by 31 ones), and the AND is 0 again. Python ints are unbounded, so -2147483648 - 1 is simply -2147483649, but the n > 0 check is still what rules negatives out.

Related tricks: n & -n isolates the lowest set bit (in two's complement, -n is ~n + 1, the bits flipped plus one); a power of four is a power of two whose bit sits in an even position, (n & 0x55555555) != 0; and BitOperations.IsPow2 in C# or n > 0 and n.bit_count() == 1 in Python do it for you.

The visualization shows n and n - 1 for 8, then 12.

starterCode.python:
def is_power_of_two(n):
    # TODO: a power of two is positive and has exactly one 1 bit.
    # n & (n - 1) clears the lowest 1 bit.
    return n % 2 == 0

visualizationSteps.message: n = 8 is 1000: one 1 bit. n - 1 = 7 is 0111: the 1 became 0 and every zero below it became 1 (1 bits in green).
8 & 7: no column has a 1 in both rows, so the AND is 0000. n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0: a power of two.
n = 12 is 1100: two 1 bits. n - 1 = 11 is 1011: only the LOWEST 1 (the 4s bit) and the zeros below it changed.
12 & 11 = 1000 = 8: the higher 1 bit survives. Not zero, so 12 is not a power of two. In general n & (n - 1) is n with its lowest 1 bit cleared.

recognitionSignals: "Is n a power of two", "exactly one bit set", or sizes that must be powers of two (hash table capacities, buffer sizes).
A follow-up asks for O(1) without loops or recursion.
Anything about the lowest set bit: n & (n - 1) clears it, n & -n keeps only it.
gotchas: Check n > 0 first: 0 and, in C#, int.MinValue both pass the bare (n & (n - 1)) == 0 test.

In C#, == binds tighter than &, so n & (n - 1) == 0 means n & ((n - 1) == 0) and doesn't compile for ints: write (n & (n - 1)) == 0. Python is the other way round (& binds tighter than ==), so the unbracketed form happens to work there, but the brackets cost nothing.
Comparing with Math.Log(n, 2) and rounding is fragile: floating-point logs aren't exact.
confusableWith: Count Set Bits (Patterns track) uses n & (n - 1) in a loop to count ones; here you only need to know whether a second one exists.
Power of Three has no bit trick (3 doesn't line up with binary); the O(1) answer there is checking whether the largest power of three in range is divisible by n.

complexity.note: One subtraction, one AND and two comparisons. (The divide-by-two loop would be O(log n).)
